strengths: Strong engineering contribution: warm-started grow-shrink and Cholesky rank-one score updates yield substantial (>100x) speedups over BOSS while preserving theoretical guarantees (Markovianity in the sample limit), enabling order-based discrete search to scale to hundreds of nodes.

Comprehensive and honest empirical evaluation across many settings (ER, scale-free, several bnlearn real-world networks, path graphs, varying noise distributions, standardized/unstandardized data, DaO sampling), including reporting of cases where FLOP and all baselines fail (e.g., Pathfinder network, dense graphs with few samples), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.

The principled initial-order construction and ILS restart mechanism are simple, well-motivated additions that measurably improve accuracy, and the paper clearly demonstrates the run-time/accuracy trade-off by varying the ILS budget.

The work engages substantively with the ongoing debate about NP-hardness rhetoric and continuous relaxation methods, providing empirical evidence (BIC and DAGMA-loss comparisons) that discrete search is competitive with or superior to state-of-the-art continuous approaches like DAGMA.
Provides a usable Rust implementation with bindings to Python/R, aiding reproducibility, and includes clear proofs for the theoretical claims about correctness of the modified grow-shrink procedure.
weaknesses: The method and its theoretical guarantees are restricted to linear (Gaussian) additive noise models; no discussion or empirical evidence is given for how the approach might extend to nonlinear or discrete-variable settings, limiting generality.

Runtime comparisons are not fully controlled: FLOP is single-threaded Rust while comparison methods (BOSS, PC, GES via Tetrad) are multithreaded Java, and the paper explicitly acknowledges this is 'not apples-to-apples,' making it hard to disentangle algorithmic gains from implementation/engineering gains.

The core algorithmic contributions (warm-start grow-shrink, Cholesky updates, correlation-based initial order, ILS with reinsertion moves) are largely incremental engineering refinements on top of existing methods (BOSS/GRaSP, standard ILS metaheuristics, standard Cholesky update routines), rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The paper does not compare against other recent methods explicitly mentioned as strong local-optima-escaping heuristics in the introduction (e.g., simulated annealing approaches of Kuipers et al., 2022), leaving the empirical comparison incomplete relative to the related work discussed.

The strong claim that 'optimizing the BIC is largely solved' on widely used linear benchmarks is somewhat overstated given the paper's own results showing failure on denser graphs, larger real-world networks (Pathfinder), and settings with fewer samples relative to graph density.

The practical guidance on selecting the ILS restart budget (a critical hyperparameter for the run-time/accuracy trade-off) is limited; in real applications without a known ground truth, it is unclear how a practitioner would choose this parameter or know when to stop.

strengths: The Cholesky-update speedup for BIC score computation (Section 3.2) is a nice, generically applicable engineering contribution that could benefit other score-based hill-climbing methods (GES, etc.), not just FLOP.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many settings: ER/SF graphs of varying size and density, path graphs, several bnlearn real-world networks (Mildew, Barley, Pathfinder, Alarm), uniform noise, unstandardized data, and the DaO simulation protocol -- this breadth is commendable.

The paper is scientifically honest about failure cases: it explicitly reports settings (Pathfinder, DaO data, dense small-sample ER graphs) where none of the methods, including FLOP, recover the ground-truth CPDAG, and it investigates why (BIC non-identifiability, faithfulness violations) rather than cherry-picking favorable results.
Reasonable theoretical grounding for the warm-started grow-shrink modification (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3), giving some asymptotic correctness guarantee for the practical speedup.
The run-time improvements over BOSS (>100x on 100-node graphs, scaling to 500 nodes where BOSS times out) are substantial and well demonstrated in Figure 2.
Useful discussion connecting compute budget to accuracy (ILS restarts) and a reasonable critique of when NP-hardness results do/do not apply to typical sparse-DAG discovery settings.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is limited: FLOP is explicitly built on top of BOSS's reinsertion/order-search framework and Iterated Local Search is a generic, well-known metaheuristic; the paper's main contributions are largely speed/engineering optimizations (warm-started grow-shrink, Cholesky updates) rather than a fundamentally new search or scoring paradigm.

Scope is narrow: the method and its theoretical guarantees are restricted to linear (Gaussian) additive noise models with BIC; the broad rhetorical claim in the title/abstract ('a reasonable approach to causal structure learning') is not well supported by experiments confined almost entirely to linear ANM synthetic and semi-synthetic (bnlearn-parameterized) data.

The favorable run-time comparisons against BOSS/PC/GES/DAGMA are partly confounded by implementation differences (single-threaded Rust vs. multithreaded Java for competitors, as the authors themselves acknowledge), complicating a fully fair apples-to-apples comparison.

No experiments on genuine real-world observational data with unknown/partially known ground truth; all 'real-world' networks are just used as DAG skeletons for synthetic data generation, so external validity claims are unsubstantiated.

The theoretical results (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3) are relatively straightforward extensions of prior grow-shrink/Markov boundary results (Margaritis 2003; Lam et al. 2022) and do not add substantial new theoretical insight beyond adapting known correctness proofs to a warm-started variant.

Baseline hyperparameters (e.g., DAGMA's lambda, PC's alpha) are fixed at 'standard' values without tuning, which could bias comparisons; similarly, ILS perturbation strength (k = ln p) and other FLOP hyperparameters are chosen based on what 'works well' without a systematic sensitivity analysis in the main text.

The paper's broader positioning as a 'call to revisit discrete search' is more of an advocacy/position statement, and while interesting, this framing arguably overstates what is fundamentally an incremental, though solid, systems contribution over an existing strong baseline (BOSS).

strengths: Strong engineering contribution: warm-started grow-shrink reinitialized from previous parent sets plus O(k^2) rank-one Cholesky updates yield >100x speedups over BOSS while preserving correctness guarantees (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3 establish that FLOP still returns a Markovian/sparsest DAG in the sample limit).

Speedups are leveraged meaningfully: the paper demonstrates a clear, well-motivated pipeline where faster local moves directly translate into more ILS restarts and measurably better accuracy (Figures 1, 3, 4), making the run-time/accuracy trade-off explicit and tunable.

Identifies and addresses a previously undiscussed practical failure mode of order-based search on path graphs (weak marginal dependence between far-apart ancestor-descendant pairs), with a simple, efficient fix (correlation-based initial order via incremental Cholesky) that is empirically validated.

Extensive and honest empirical evaluation across many settings: ER/SF random graphs at multiple densities and sizes (up to 500 nodes), real bnlearn networks (Alarm, Mildew, Barley, Pathfinder), uniform noise, unstandardized data, DaO sampling, and dense low-sample regimes, with SHD, AID, and BIC-score comparisons.

Candid reporting of failure cases and limitations (e.g., Pathfinder network where more ILS search improves BIC but worsens SHD, suggesting BIC non-identifiability at the given sample size), which strengthens scientific credibility rather than overselling results.

Useful ablation isolating the contribution of each speedup component (Figure 2) and a fair-ish comparison against BOSS with random restarts and an exact solver, showing FLOP approaches exact-search quality at much lower cost.
Practical contribution of a ready-to-use Rust implementation callable from Python/R, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic ingredients (order-based reinsertion search from BOSS, grow-shrink, ILS as a generic metaheuristic, Cholesky-based score updates) are individually well-established; the novelty here is largely in their careful combination and systems-level optimization rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical idea.

Runtime comparisons against BOSS are explicitly acknowledged as not apples-to-apples (Rust single-threaded vs. Java multithreaded Tetrad), which somewhat undercuts the strength of the headline speedup claims even though the paper is transparent about this.

The comparison to BOSS in the ILS experiments uses only full independent restarts as the escape mechanism for BOSS, which is a relatively weak baseline for escaping local optima; a more sophisticated perturbation-based ILS variant of BOSS was not implemented/tested, making the FLOP vs. BOSS ILS comparison somewhat asymmetric.

No theoretical analysis of ILS convergence rates or of how the perturbation parameter k should scale with graph properties beyond the heuristic default k = ln(p); sensitivity of results to this hyperparameter is not explored.

The paper's broader rhetorical claims (e.g., that NP-hardness concerns are largely inapplicable and that BIC optimization is 'largely solved' on standard benchmarks) are stronger than what the restricted linear-Gaussian, moderate-density synthetic benchmark evidence fully supports, and could be tempered given the Pathfinder/DaO counterexamples reported in the appendix.

The method and evaluation are restricted to linear (Gaussian/uniform-noise) ANMs and the BIC score; no extension or discussion of nonlinear models, discrete/mixed data, or alternative scores, limiting the generality of the claimed impact.

Some comparisons (e.g., other strong order-based competitors like GRaSP) are mentioned in related work but not included as empirical baselines, leaving open how FLOP compares against the full state of the art in order-based discrete search.

strengths: Strong, extensive empirical evaluation across many settings (ER, SF, path, dense graphs, bnlearn networks, causalAssembly, Sachs, non-linear misspecified settings, varying sample sizes and parameters), with SHD, AID, and BIC-based analyses, lending good support to the central claims.

Concrete, well-motivated algorithmic contributions: warm-started non-greedy grow-shrink with a theoretical guarantee (Markov boundary correctness under warm start) and Cholesky rank-one update/downdate for local BIC scoring, yielding large empirical speedups over BOSS (>100x at 100 nodes) while scaling to 500 nodes.
The principled initial-order construction addressing weak long-range dependence in path-like structures is a useful, previously underdiscussed practical fix, with clear empirical benefit.

Honest and thorough discussion of failure modes: cases where the BIC optimum does not correspond to the true CPDAG (non-identifiability, faithfulness violations, non-linear misspecification), including the Pathfinder and Onion-method examples where more search leads to worse SHD despite better score, which is a valuable and rare kind of transparency.
Practical contribution of a fast, open-source Rust implementation (pip-installable), increasing potential impact and reproducibility.

The paper engages critically and substantively with the discrete-vs-continuous optimization debate in causal discovery, including a useful empirical point that FLOP-recovered graphs achieve lower DAGMA loss than DAGMA itself, questioning claimed optimization advantages of continuous relaxations.
weaknesses: Core algorithmic contribution is largely an engineering acceleration (warm-starts, Cholesky updates, principled initialization, ILS) layered on top of the pre-existing BOSS/order-search paradigm; the conceptual novelty relative to BOSS, GRaSP, and existing ILS use in causal discovery (Liu et al. 2023; Nazaret & Blei 2024) is comparatively modest.

The headline run-time comparisons against BOSS use a Java/multithreaded Tetrad implementation vs. a Rust/single-threaded FLOP implementation, which the authors themselves flag as not apples-to-apples; this weakens the strength of the speed claims and makes it hard to disentangle implementation-language effects from algorithmic gains.

No baseline comparison against more recent competitive order-based search methods explicitly cited as strong performers (e.g., Li et al. 2025), despite the paper's framing suggesting FLOP should be benchmarked against the state of the art in order-based local search, not only BOSS/PC/GES/DAGMA.

The method and theoretical guarantees are restricted to linear Gaussian ANMs with the BIC score; robustness experiments (non-linear, semi-synthetic, real data) show substantial performance degradation or score misspecification, somewhat undercutting the broader rhetorical claims in the abstract/discussion about discrete search being generally "reasonable" for causal discovery.

Some of the rhetorical framing (e.g., "recalibrating what is considered hard," dismissing NP-hardness concerns) is broad and could be seen as overreaching given the narrow linear-Gaussian, causally-sufficient setting under which the strong results hold.

Scalability, while improved over BOSS, is still limited to hundreds of variables under moderate time budgets; the practical relevance to real-world high-dimensional causal discovery problems (thousands of variables) remains unclear.

The ILS perturbation strategy (random swaps with k=ln p) and BIC penalty choice are essentially treated as fixed hyperparameters validated only via post-hoc plots (Appendix C.10) rather than a principled selection procedure, offering limited guidance for out-of-distribution problems where good defaults may not transfer.

strengths: The Cholesky rank-one update trick for incremental BIC scoring during local search is a genuinely useful, well-explained engineering contribution that is broadly applicable beyond this paper's specific algorithm (e.g., to GES or other hill-climbers).

Very extensive empirical evaluation: dozens of settings covering ER/SF graphs, bnlearn networks (Mildew, Barley, Pathfinder, Alarm), real semi-synthetic data (causalAssembly), real data (Sachs), non-linear misspecification (MLP/GP), varying sample sizes, graph sizes up to 500 nodes, and multiple accuracy metrics (SHD, AID, BIC gap).

The paper is commendably self-critical: it reports cases where its own method's BIC-optimal graphs diverge from the ground truth (e.g., Onion-sampled data, Pathfinder, dense low-sample ER graphs), rather than only showcasing favorable results.

Correctness arguments for the warm-started, non-greedy grow-shrink procedure (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3) give some theoretical grounding that the modifications do not sacrifice the asymptotic Markovianity guarantee.
Practical artifact: a Rust implementation with a pip-installable package, aiding reproducibility and adoption.

The ablation isolating the two speed contributions (warm-start grow-shrink vs. Cholesky updates) and the two accuracy contributions (initial order vs. ILS) is clear and convincing for the claims it makes about run-time and accuracy improvements over BOSS.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is incremental: FLOP is essentially BOSS (reinsertion/order search) plus (a) a warm-started, non-greedy grow-shrink, (b) Cholesky rank-one updates, (c) a heuristic initial-order construction, and (d) a standard ILS metaheuristic applied to the order search. Each piece individually is a relatively standard optimization/engineering idea, which somewhat undercuts the paper's rhetorically strong framing ("a reasonable approach", "calls for revisiting discrete search") relative to the actual size of the methodological advance.

The method and theory are restricted to linear Gaussian ANMs with the BIC score; the appendix shows substantial accuracy degradation under misspecification (non-linear data, Onion-sampled data, Pathfinder, dense graphs with moderate sample size), which tempers the paper's broader claims about discrete search being generally "reasonable" for causal discovery in practice.

Runtime comparisons to BOSS are explicitly acknowledged as not apples-to-apples (Rust single-threaded FLOP vs. Java multithreaded Tetrad BOSS), which weakens the strength of the headline speed claims even though the authors are transparent about this.

Missing comparisons to other strong recent baselines that the introduction explicitly cites as top performers (e.g., GRaSP, simulated-annealing-based methods, the more recent order-based local search of Li et al. 2025) — only BOSS, PC, GES, and DAGMA (and occasionally LiNGAM/GOLEM) are benchmarked, leaving open whether FLOP's gains hold against the strongest existing competitors.

On harder regimes (dense graphs, low sample sizes, Pathfinder), the advantage of FLOP over BOSS and even over the exact solver narrows substantially or reverses in terms of recovery accuracy even though BIC is better optimized, which somewhat undermines the central thesis that better discrete optimization straightforwardly yields better causal discovery.

The theoretical results (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3) are relatively direct extensions of prior grow-shrink correctness arguments (Margaritis 2003; Lam et al. 2022) rather than a substantial new theoretical contribution.

The scope is limited to the causal-sufficiency, CPDAG-identifiable setting under linear Gaussian noise with asymptotic faithfulness; the paper does not engage with latent confounding or more general real-world complications beyond citing them in the discussion, so the practical significance of the contribution outside well-specified synthetic benchmarks remains unclear.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated technical contributions: warm-started grow-shrink reusing previous parent sets, dynamic Cholesky rank-one updates for local score computation, a principled correlation-based initial order construction, and an iterated local search (ILS) metaheuristic. Each component is well explained and individually justified.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper proves that the modified grow-shrink procedure still recovers the restricted Markov boundary and that FLOP returns a Markovian CPDAG in the sample limit, extending existing GRaSP/BOSS theory to the warm-start/non-greedy setting.

Substantial and rigorous empirical evaluation: benchmarks span ER/SF graphs at multiple densities and sizes (up to 500 nodes), several bnlearn networks (Alarm, Mildew, Barley, Pathfinder), semi-synthetic (causalAssembly) and real (Sachs) data, as well as robustness checks for non-Gaussian noise, unstandardized data, non-linear misspecification, and alternative data-generating procedures (Onion method). This breadth is unusually thorough for the area.

Demonstrates large, clearly quantified run-time improvements (>100x over BOSS at 100 nodes) while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy (SHD/AID), including near-exact recovery on several benchmarks.

Honest and insightful discussion of when BIC-optimal graphs do not coincide with the ground truth (finite-sample non-identifiability), which tempers the paper's own claims and adds scientific value beyond just presenting a faster algorithm.
Practical contribution: an available Rust implementation with a Python package, aiding reproducibility and adoption.

The paper engages critically and specifically with the NP-hardness rhetoric and continuous-relaxation literature, providing concrete counter-evidence (e.g., DAGMA's own loss is better optimized by FLOP's solution) that adds a useful critical perspective to the field.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic framework (order-based search with reinsertion, grow-shrink) is inherited from BOSS/GRaSP; the novelty is largely in engineering/optimization speedups (warm starts, Cholesky updates) and a heuristic initialization/ILS scheme rather than a fundamentally new search paradigm, which somewhat tempers the conceptual contribution relative to the framing ('embracing discrete search' as a broad claim).

The method and theory are restricted to linear (Gaussian) ANMs with the BIC score; extension to nonlinear or discrete settings is not addressed, limiting the generality of the claims despite the paper's broad rhetorical framing about causal discovery generally.

Some theoretical results (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3) are relatively direct adaptations of prior grow-shrink/Markov-boundary correctness proofs and provide only asymptotic guarantees, which do not directly explain or guarantee the strong finite-sample performance that is the paper's main empirical claim.

Comparisons to very recent competitive order-based methods (e.g., Li et al. 2025, referenced in intro) are not included in the main experiments, leaving open how FLOP compares to the most recent state of the art rather than just BOSS/PC/GES/DAGMA.

On real/semi-synthetic data (causalAssembly, Sachs, Pathfinder) performance gains are modest or absent, and in several cases (Pathfinder, DAO-sampled data) more aggressive optimization (higher ILS budget) actually worsens recovery, suggesting the practical utility of the proposed aggressive search is uncertain outside idealized synthetic settings — a point the paper acknowledges but which still limits the significance of the central claim.

The ILS perturbation scheme and its default hyperparameter (k = ln p swaps) are justified mostly empirically on specific instance classes (Figure 14) without a more systematic or theoretical treatment of sensitivity across diverse graph structures/densities.

Runtime comparisons with BOSS are explicitly noted as not apples-to-apples (Rust/single-thread vs Java/multithreaded Tetrad), which, while acknowledged, makes the headline speed-up numbers somewhat less rigorous as a controlled comparison.
